query: Consider the following context: Temper embrittlement, characterized by a dramatic loss of ductility within a narrow temperature window, is ubiquitous in conventional alloys but is not reported in compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems. In that context, which material can be used for ductile–brittle–ductile transition, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Conventional alloys with a specific composition and processing history can exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition when subjected to a controlled temperature variation within a narrow temperature window, whereas compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems do not exhibit this behavior due to their inherent resistance to temper embrittlement.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional alloy with a specific composition (e.g., Fe-Cr-Ni) and processing history (e.g., annealed at 1000°C for 1 hour)
generation.intervention: Temperature variation within a narrow temperature window (e.g., 200-400°C) at a rate of 5°C/min
generation.conditions: Uniaxial tensile testing with a strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary segregation of impurities (e.g., P, S) and the resulting formation of brittle phases
generation.mechanism: Thermally activated diffusion of impurities to grain boundaries, leading to the formation of brittle phases and a loss of ductility
generation.predicted_outcome: A 30% reduction in ductility (measured as elongation to failure) at the peak embrittlement temperature, relative to the ductility at 200°C
generation.baseline: Ductility of the conventional alloy at 200°C (e.g., 20% elongation to failure)
generation.uncertainty: The exact composition and processing history of the conventional alloy, as well as the specific impurities and brittle phases involved, may affect the magnitude and temperature range of the ductile–brittle–ductile transition

falsification_experiment.design: Uniaxial tensile testing of conventional alloys with varying compositions and processing histories, subjected to temperature variations within the narrow temperature window
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ductility of the conventional alloy does not decrease by at least 20% at the peak embrittlement temperature, relative to the ductility at 200°C, then the hypothesis is falsified

system.material: conventional alloys vs compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems

frame.limitation: conventional alloys exhibit temper embrittlement, while compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems do not
root_cause_cues: compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems
constraints: conventional alloys vs compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems

precedents.lever: in situ neutron diffraction and compressive testing
precedents.outcome: The alloy exhibits a single BCC solid solution phase stable up to 900°C with grain sizes of 200 to 400 μm.

precedents.problem: Designing high-entropy alloys for high Snoek-type damping capacity, high mechanical strength, and high ductility
precedents.outcome: The O-2 HEA achieved a peak damping capacity (tanδ_max) of 0.020 at 1.0 Hz, while the N-2 HEA reached 0.027 at 1.0 Hz.

precedents.problem: Improving strength and ductility in refractory high-entropy alloys
precedents.outcome: The alloy achieved an ultrahigh ultimate tensile strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature.

precedents.problem: Synergy between strength and ductility in refractory high-entropy alloys
precedents.outcome: The addition of 4.2 at% Cr led to the formation of a Laves phase in addition to the BCC phase, resulting in improved hardness and yield strength.

precedents.problem: Improving room temperature ductility in refractory high-entropy alloys
precedents.outcome: Condition (3) achieved an 'inverted' microstructure with a continuous disordered BCC matrix and discrete ~50 nm B2 precipitates, yielding 1345 MPa and 38% compressive fracture strain at room temperature.

precedents.problem: Overcoming strength-ductility trade-off in eutectic high entropy alloys
precedents.outcome: The HPHT-treated alloy achieved a tensile strength of 1150 MPa and a tensile ductility of 36%, representing a doubling of both properties compared to the precursor.

precedents.problem: Temperature-dependent mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys
precedents.lever: Selective laser melting and mechanical testing
precedents.outcome: The SLM-built HEA exhibited a yield strength of 778.4 MPa at room temperature, significantly higher than annealed and other AM-processed variants.

precedents.problem: Additive manufacturing of refractory high-entropy alloys
precedents.outcome: The sintered bulk samples exhibit a yield strength significantly higher than arc-melted HfNbTaTiZr and Inconel 718 between 750 and 1100 °C.

precedents.problem: Designing high-entropy alloys for high fracture strength and ductility
precedents.outcome: The as-cast alloy exhibited a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure with an inter-lamellar spacing of about 2 μm, and a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6% at room temperature.
